idiom_name: NestJS @Render view engine + serializer/DTO per representation
implementation_notes: Nest keeps the model in the controller: @Render('movie') with a template engine configured through setViewEngine returns the HTML representation, while the same service result returned as a plain object is serialized by the platform (Express res.json, Fastify serializer) for the API representation, and injecting @Res()/@Reply() lets the handler negotiate explicitly with res.render()/res.format()/reply.view(). ClassSerializerInterceptor with @Exclude/@Expose plus a DTO interface per representation is the shared projection that keeps the JSON from exposing what the template hides. TypeScript types do not enforce this at run time, so the DTO boundary is the actual contract.
pitfalls: Using @Res()/@Reply() disables Nest's response pipeline: the handler must finish the response itself, and errors thrown after the response has started are no longer converted into the usual error payload.
Annotating the domain entity with class-transformer decorators couples the model to one representation; 'hidden in the template' does not hide a field from the JSON payload.
Template engines are configured in bootstrap and are global to the Nest application, so end-to-end tests can render stale templates unless each test builds its own application.
